q: Name one type of atmospheric hazard.
a: Tropical storms / droughts / floods

q: Name one type of tectonic hazard.
a: Earthquake / volcanic eruption / tsunami

q: What is an earthquake?
a: Violent shaking of the Earth's crust due to movement of the Earth's plates

q: What is a volcanic eruption?
a: Violent eruption of lava and ash from a volcano

q: What is a plate boundary?
a: A place where two plates meet

q: What happens at a destructive plate boundary?
a: Plates move together and crust is destroyed

q: What happens at a constructive plate boundary?
a: Plates move apart and new crust is created

q: What happens at a conservative plate boundary?
a: Plates slide past each other, pressure builds up and is released as an earthquake

q: What is a primary effect?
a: An effect that happens straight away, e.g. buildings collapse, people killed, roads damaged

q: What is a secondary effect?
a: An effect that occurs later as a result of the primary effects, e.g. disease spreads in camps, landslides

q: Give one example of a secondary effect of a tectonic hazard.
a: Disease spreads in camps / landslides triggered / agriculture destroyed / people left without power

q: What is an immediate response?
a: Something that happens in the hours or days after a disaster, e.g. distributing food and water, rescuing people from rubble

q: What is the management of hazards?
a: Trying to make sure fewer people are killed next time

q: Which can be predicted: volcanoes or earthquakes?
a: Volcanoes can be predicted, earthquakes cannot

q: Give one way of protecting people from earthquakes.
a: Earthquake resistant buildings / shutting off gas pipelines

q: Give one way of planning for earthquakes.
a: Earthquake drills / evacuation plans

q: What do sensors pick up when monitoring an earthquake zone?
a: Foreshocks

q: Name one factor affecting hazard risk.
a: Location (how close to a plate margin) / level of development / urban or rural area

q: Why do more people die in urban areas?
a: More people live there

q: What is the difference between weather and climate?
a: Weather is the atmospheric conditions in a place on one day; climate is weather conditions over a long period of time

q: What is a tropical storm?
a: An area of low pressure with winds blowing around a central calm point called the eye

q: Between which latitudes are tropical storms found?
a: Between 5° and 30° north and south of the Equator

q: What is a tropical storm called in North America and the Caribbean?
a: A hurricane

q: State one condition needed for a tropical storm to form.
a: Sea over 27°C / water vapour in the atmosphere / low pressure / Coriolis effect

q: What is the Coriolis effect?
a: The spinning of the Earth

q: What is the eye of a tropical storm like?
a: The middle of the storm, where conditions are calm

q: Where are the strongest winds in a tropical storm?
a: The eye wall, at the edge of the eye

q: What are the weather conditions in a tropical storm?
a: Strong winds (up to 250 km/h), very heavy rain and storm surges

q: How is climate change affecting tropical storms?
a: The sea is warming and the number of storms is increasing

q: Give one way of protecting people from tropical storms.
a: Storm shelters / storm resistant homes / hurricane straps on roofs / storm shutters

q: Give one way of planning for tropical storms.
a: Early warning systems / disaster supply kits / evacuation / building bans in high risk areas

q: How are satellites used to manage tropical storms?
a: To track the storm's progress (monitoring and prediction)

q: What is flooding?
a: When a river bursts its banks and water spills onto the floodplain

q: How long ago did the Quaternary period start?
a: 2.6 million years ago

q: What caused climate change in the Quaternary?
a: Natural (physical) causes

q: What is the enhanced greenhouse effect?
a: Humans produce more greenhouse gases, the layer thickens, more heat is trapped and the Earth gets warmer

q: What are Milankovitch cycles?
a: Changes in the Earth's orbit (every 100,000 years) and tilt (every 41,000 years)

q: What are sunspots?
a: Dark patches on the surface of the sun that may make it shine less brightly

q: How can volcanic activity change the climate?
a: Ash in the atmosphere may block the sun's heat (global dimming)

q: How does agriculture contribute to climate change?
a: It is responsible for about 20% of greenhouse emissions; cattle produce methane

q: Give one effect of climate change on people.
a: Crop yields decrease in some places / increased risk of heat stroke and skin cancer

q: Give one effect of climate change on the environment.
a: More extreme weather / sea level rise / desertification

q: What is mitigation?
a: Trying to reduce our carbon emissions

q: Give one example of mitigation.
a: Using renewable energy / encouraging cycling (Mini-Holland scheme in Walthamstow)

q: What is adaptation?
a: Making changes to cope with climate change

q: Give one example of adaptation.
a: Building flood defences (Thames Barrier) / storing grain for droughts

q: Why are hot deserts never found on the Equator?
a: They are found along the tropics of Cancer and Capricorn, around 30° north and south

q: Why is the rainfall in hot deserts described as unreliable?
a: Deserts can go years with no rain

q: What are desert soils like?
a: Sandy and rocky, with very little organic content because of the lack of vegetation

q: Give one challenge in hot deserts.
a: Extreme temperatures / water supply / inaccessibility

q: Why is water supply a challenge in the Sahara?
a: Under 20 mm of rain a year, oases are far apart and most water is deep underground in aquifers

q: Why is inaccessibility a challenge in the Sahara?
a: There are very few roads

q: What is desertification?
a: When previously fertile land on the edge of a desert turns into desert

q: Give one cause of desertification.
a: Overgrazing / over-cultivation / population growth / climate change

q: What is overgrazing?
a: Too many animals on the land, so it becomes bare and the soil compacted

q: What is over-cultivation?
a: Too many crops grown, so the land does not recover and the soil becomes infertile

q: Give one way of managing desertification.
a: Tree planting / appropriate technology such as solar cookers / water management such as bunds

q: How do bunds help to manage desertification?
a: Low stone walls slow the flow of water over dry ground and prevent soil erosion

q: How do solar cookers help to manage desertification?
a: They stop poor women cutting down trees for firewood

q: How do camels survive in the desert?
a: Fatty hump stores energy, fat in one place stops overheating, and they sweat very little

q: How does the saguaro cactus survive in the desert?
a: Large fleshy stems store water and no leaves reduce water loss through transpiration

q: How does the ocotillo plant survive in the desert?
a: It is dormant in dry periods and flowers after rain

q: Why are lizards and snakes only active in the early morning?
a: To avoid the heat of the day

q: What is an ephemeral plant?
a: One that changes its behaviour to survive, e.g. only flowering after heavy rain

q: What is a drainage basin?
a: The area of land drained by a river

q: What is a watershed?
a: The edge of the drainage basin, which is high land

q: What is a confluence?
a: Where a tributary meets the main channel

q: What is a tributary?
a: A smaller river that joins the main channel

q: What is hydraulic action?
a: Erosion through the power of water

q: What is abrasion?
a: Rocks carried by the river wear away the bed and banks

q: What is attrition?
a: Rocks carried by the river smash together and become smoother and smaller

q: What is solution?
a: Rocks dissolve in river water

q: What is vertical erosion?
a: The river erodes downwards, mostly in the upper course, creating a V-shaped valley

q: What is lateral erosion?
a: The river erodes sideways, mostly in the middle and lower course

q: What is traction?
a: Large particles rolled along the river bed

q: What is suspension?
a: Even smaller particles are carried in the river water

q: Name one landform of the upper course.
a: Interlocking spurs / waterfalls / gorges

q: Name one landform of the lower course.
a: Levees / floodplains / estuaries

q: What is a long profile?
a: The steepness of a river from source to mouth

q: What is a cross profile?
a: A slice through the river valley

q: What is surface run-off?
a: Water travelling over the ground to the channel, the fastest way water travels

q: What is throughflow?
a: Water travelling through the soil to the channel

q: What is groundwater flow?
a: Water travelling through rock to the channel, the slowest way

q: What is hard engineering?
a: Using man-made structures to control natural processes

q: What is soft engineering?
a: Working with natural processes to manage flood risk

q: Give one example of hard engineering on a river.
a: Dams and reservoirs / channel straightening / embankments / flood relief channels

q: Give one example of soft engineering on a river.
a: Flood warnings and preparation / flood plain zoning / planting trees / river restoration

q: What is flood plain zoning?
a: People are not allowed to build on areas likely to flood

q: What is swash?
a: A wave moving up the beach

q: What is backwash?
a: A wave moving back down the beach

q: What are constructive waves like?
a: Low and gentle, with swash more powerful than backwash, so they deposit material

q: What are destructive waves like?
a: Tall storm waves, high frequency, with backwash stronger than swash, so they remove material

q: What is hydraulic power on a coast?
a: Waves smash against the cliff and trapped air is forced into cracks

q: What is longshore drift?
a: Sediment transported along the coast in a zigzag pattern when the prevailing wind hits at an angle

q: How is a wave-cut platform formed?
a: Destructive waves undercut the base of the cliff, creating a notch, until the cliff collapses

q: Put in order: stack, arch, stump, cave.
a: Cave, arch, stack, stump

q: What is freeze-thaw weathering?
a: Water collects in cracks, freezes and expands, and breaks off rock

q: What is salt weathering?
a: Seawater evaporates in cracks leaving salt crystals that expand and break off rock

q: What is carbonation?
a: Acidic rainwater attacks alkaline rocks like limestone

q: What is mass movement?
a: The downward movement or sliding of material under gravity

q: What is a rockfall?
a: Fragments of rock break away from a cliff because of freeze-thaw weathering

q: What is slumping?
a: Saturated soil and weak rock slump along a weak point

q: Where do beaches form?
a: In sheltered bays, where low energy waves deposit sediment

q: How does a spit form?
a: Longshore drift continues as the coast changes direction

q: How does a bar form?
a: Longshore drift continues across a bay

q: Give one advantage of sea walls.
a: Very effective

q: Give one disadvantage of sea walls.
a: Expensive / obtrusive / block access to the beach

q: Give one advantage of rock armour.
a: Cheap

q: Give one disadvantage of rock armour.
a: Obtrusive / unattractive / rocks come from abroad

q: Give one advantage of groynes.
a: They create a wider beach and stop the beach being removed

q: Give one disadvantage of groynes.
a: They starve the beach further along the coast of sediment / unnatural / unattractive

q: Give one advantage of beach nourishment.
a: Cheap / blends in with the existing beach / sand is a natural defence

q: Give one disadvantage of beach nourishment.
a: Needs constant maintenance

q: Give one advantage of dune regeneration.
a: Looks natural / dunes are a natural sea defence

q: Give one disadvantage of dune regeneration.
a: Can be damaged by storms

q: Give one advantage of managed retreat.
a: Saves money in the long term / can create new habitats such as salt marsh

q: Give one disadvantage of managed retreat.
a: Some landowners, such as farmers, are angry

q: When did more people first live in cities than in the countryside?
What is counter urbanisation?
a: People leave the city because of traffic congestion or a lack of affordable housing

q: What is urban sprawl?
a: The unplanned growth of cities into the countryside

q: What is a squatter settlement?
a: An area of poor quality, illegally built housing in an LIC city

q: Give one reason why LIC cities are growing quickly.
a: Rural-urban migration / natural increase

q: What is a push factor?
a: A negative thing driving you away from a place, e.g. lack of services

q: What is a pull factor?
a: A positive thing pulling you towards a place, e.g. higher-paid jobs

q: Give one challenge of living in LIC and NEE cities.
a: Slums / clean water and sewage / waste disposal / air pollution and traffic congestion

q: What does CBD stand for?
a: Central business district

q: What is the inner city like?
a: Next to the CBD, traditionally factories and working class terraced housing or high rise blocks

q: What are suburbs like?
a: Towards the edge of the city, mainly residential, bigger semi-detached housing and more green space

q: What is the rural-urban fringe?
a: The edge of the city, a transition zone between the city and the countryside

q: What is a commuter settlement?
a: A town or village where people live but many travel to another city to work

q: What is urban deprivation?
a: Poverty, including high unemployment, poor housing, poor health and low educational achievement

q: What is regeneration?
a: Planned improvements to the built environment, also designed to reduce unemployment in deprived areas

q: What is dereliction?
a: Factories in inner city areas are abandoned and buildings get into a worse and worse condition

q: What is urban greening?
a: Creating more green space in cities, e.g. green roofs and parklets

q: Give one benefit of urban greening.
a: Reduces flooding / trees and plants are carbon sinks

q: What is urban sustainability?
a: Building cities that provide for residents today without compromising the needs of future generations

q: What is a greenfield site?
a: A site that has not previously been built on, e.g. farmland or woodland

q: Give one advantage of building on greenfield sites.
a: Land is cheaper in rural areas

q: Give one disadvantage of building on greenfield sites.
a: Increases urban sprawl and ecosystems are lost

q: Give one advantage of building on brownfield sites.
a: Sites are available since industry declined

q: Give one disadvantage of building on brownfield sites.
a: Old buildings need demolishing first / land may be contaminated

q: What is development?
a: Progress in a country's quality of life and standard of living

q: What is GNI per head?
a: Gross National Income divided by the population

q: What is standard of living?
a: How much money and material wealth people have

q: What is quality of life?
a: How good life feels and how satisfied people are

q: What is a problem with GNI per head?
a: It is an average, so it hides gaps between rich and poor

q: What is an NEE?
a: A country that is developing fast, with its economy shifting from primary to secondary industry

q: What is the development gap?
a: The economic and social gap between the world's richest and poorest countries

q: What is infant mortality?
a: The number of babies under 1 who die per 1,000

q: What does HDI measure?
a: Life expectancy, education and GNI per capita, scored 0 to 1

q: What is a TNC?
a: A company that operates in more than one country

q: What is the positive multiplier effect?
a: A TNC opens, jobs are created, people spend more locally, tax rises, and this attracts more investment

q: What is aid?
a: Money, goods or expertise from governments, organisations or charities

q: Give one advantage of foreign investment.
a: Foreign companies bring money and expertise / jobs / tax

q: Give one disadvantage of foreign investment.
a: Profits flow out of the country (economic leakage) / TNCs sometimes do not pay tax

q: Give one advantage of aid.
a: Can be used in hospitals and schools / quick help in emergencies

q: Give one disadvantage of aid.
a: Loans must be paid back with interest / dependency / money lost to corruption

q: Give one advantage of tourism for development.
a: Creates direct and indirect jobs / more money for infrastructure

q: Give one disadvantage of tourism for development.
a: Economic leakage / low wage and seasonal jobs / litter and pressure on ecosystems / local prices go up

q: What is Fairtrade?
a: Farmers get a fair, guaranteed price plus money for the community (Fairtrade Premium)

q: Give one advantage of Fairtrade.
a: Stable higher incomes / better working conditions

q: Give one disadvantage of Fairtrade.
a: Products cost the consumer more

q: What is microfinance?
a: Very small loans to people who cannot get a loan from a normal bank, to start a small business

q: Give one disadvantage of microfinance.
a: Interest can be high / loans too small for big growth

q: What is debt relief?
a: Cancelling or reducing money a country owes

q: Give one advantage of debt relief.
a: Cuts interest so money can be spent on hospitals and schools

q: Give one disadvantage of debt relief.
a: Often has conditions attached

q: Which sector do most people in LICs work in?
a: Primary

q: Which sector do most people in HICs work in?
a: Tertiary

q: What is industrialisation?
a: When a country shifts to manufacturing, the secondary sector

q: What is deindustrialisation?
a: When manufacturing and heavy industry decline

q: What is a post-industrial economy?
a: An economy after deindustrialisation when most people work in services

q: What is globalisation?
a: The way the world has become more interconnected through trade, travel, foreign investment, migration and communication

q: What is the quaternary sector?
a: Jobs that create new knowledge, e.g. app designer, medical researcher

q: What is infrastructure?
a: Structures that help a country run, e.g. roads, railways, sewage systems

q: Give one reason for deindustrialisation.
a: Cheaper to manufacture abroad / strikes made factories uncompetitive / government cut subsidies

q: What is HS2?
a: A new high speed railway linking London, Birmingham, Leeds and Manchester

q: Give one advantage of HS2.
a: Easier to commute between northern cities and London / 100,000 new jobs, most outside London

q: Give one disadvantage of HS2.
a: 1000s of homes destroyed / critics say a railway will not fix the north-south divide

q: What is London Gateway?
a: A £1.5bn new mega port on the Thames estuary

q: Give one advantage of a third runway at Heathrow.
a: More passengers and exports, worth £214bn a year to the UK

q: Give one disadvantage of a third runway at Heathrow.
a: 200,000 more flights over London a year, causing more air and noise pollution

q: What is the UK's biggest export?
a: Financial services

q: Which tunnel links the UK to France?
a: The Channel Tunnel

q: What type of rural area is growing?
a: Commuter settlements near big cities, because of counter-urbanisation

q: What type of rural area is depopulating?
a: Areas far from major cities with few jobs because of the decline in manufacturing or farming

q: What is the Commonwealth?
a: A group of countries that used to be colonised by Britain, e.g. Nigeria, Canada, Jamaica

q: What is the EU?
a: A group of countries which share some laws, where citizens can live and work freely in other member countries

q: What is well-being?
a: The state of being comfortable, healthy or happy

q: What is scarcity?
a: A shortage

q: What is a carbon footprint?
a: The amount of carbon dioxide released as a result of the activities of an individual, organisation or community

q: What is energy security?
a: Having reliable, uninterrupted and affordable energy

q: What is an energy surplus?
a: When a country produces more energy than its population requires

q: What is an energy deficit?
a: Having less energy than required

q: What are fossil fuels?
a: Natural fuels formed from the remains of living things: coal, oil and gas

q: What is renewable energy?
a: Energy sources that will not run out

q: Give one reason energy consumption is increasing.
a: Rising population / economic development / technology

q: Give one advantage of solar energy.
a: Potential in LICs with lots of sunlight

q: Give one disadvantage of solar energy.
a: Farms need a lot of space / expensive / unreliable as it relies on sunlight

q: Give one advantage of hydroelectric power.
a: Flow can be controlled so electricity is generated only when there is demand

q: Give one disadvantage of hydroelectric power.
a: Damages freshwater ecosystems / land needs flooding and may displace people

q: Give one advantage of geothermal energy.
a: Cheap and reliable

q: Give one disadvantage of geothermal energy.
a: Only works in tectonically active areas

q: Give one advantage of tidal energy.
a: Reliably predicted because tide cycles are regular

q: Give one disadvantage of tidal energy.
a: Cannot generate all the time / turbines are expensive

q: Give one advantage of wind energy.
a: Cost-effective

q: Give one disadvantage of wind energy.
a: NIMBYism: people do not want them spoiling the view / expensive to build

q: What is the UK water surplus area?
a: The higher north and west, where most rain falls and population density is lower

q: What is the UK water deficit area?
a: The south and east, where low rainfall meets high population density

q: How can water pollution be managed?
a: Monitoring river quality, filtering, purifying with chlorine, restricting recreational use, strict regulations

q: What is organic farming?
a: Farming that does not use chemicals

q: What did Andy Burnham re-nationalise as mayor of Greater Manchester?
a: The buses

q: Why is the UK's weather so changeable?
a: Different air masses affect it
alt: It is affected by several air masses

q: What type of low pressure system do many storms affecting the UK begin as?
a: Depression

q: What fast-moving band of high altitude air carries depressions towards Britain?
a: The jet stream

q: Which storm brought winds of about 96 mph to Devon in December 2024?
a: Storm Darragh

q: Which storm brought 150 to 200 mm of rain to eastern Scotland in October 2023?
a: Storm Babet

q: Which area of high pressure, sitting over Britain, is linked to UK heatwaves?
a: An anticyclone

q: What is the UK's record temperature, set on 19 July 2022?
Give one way water companies respond to a drought in the UK.
a: Hosepipe bans

q: Why are cold spells in the UK expected to become less common?
a: Britain is getting warmer

q: Which type of air arriving from the east brings prolonged freezing weather to the UK?
a: Polar continental air

q: What is biodiversity?
a: The variety of plant and animal life in an area
alt: The number of different species in an area

q: In a food chain, what do secondary consumers eat?
a: Primary consumers

q: What is the term for the change in vegetation up a mountain as altitude increases?
a: Vertical zonation

q: Which warm ocean current keeps Western Europe milder than other places at the same latitude?
a: The Gulf Stream

q: What type of ocean current helps create the dry conditions of the Atacama Desert?
a: A cold current

q: What is evapotranspiration?
a: Water lost to the air from soil and plants
alt: Evaporation from the soil and transpiration from plants

q: Why are nutrients recycled so quickly in a tropical rainforest?
a: Warm, damp conditions make decomposition fast
